latin.665: GAR. His pedicis facile nos extricabimus. Etenim 1. His verbis Apostolum id confirmare, quod superiori versu dixerat, in confesso est uti iam audivimus. Dixerat autem, omnes in Adamo peccasse, quibus verbis imputationem inobedientiae actualis Adae doceri, manifestis rationibus addiximus. Itaque ratio qua id confirmat & elucidat Apostolus hoc ℣. 13. non potest non esse imputationi favorabilis.
latin.666: PLAC. Nos vero quam illae rationes nullae sint, nostris & responsionibus & rationibus ita clarum fecisse arbitramur, ut nullus sit reliquus dubitandi locus.
latin.667: GAR. 2. Argumento quod hic usurpatur adversus imputationem peccati Adae, non minus uti poterit aliquis adversus imputationem actualis obedientiae Christi. Nam si recte colligitur inobedientiam Adami non fuisse imputatam usque ad legem, quia non perduravit usque ad legem: quidni etiam legitime colligatur, actualem Christi obedientiam, qua se obedientem praestitit usque ad mortem, nobis nequaquam imputari posse, quia non duravit usque ad nostra tempora?
latin.668: PLAC. Non collegi inobedientiam Adami non fuisse imputatam usque ad legem, quia non perduravit usque ad legem. Argumentum meum, quod est invictum, Vir doctus in aliud transmutat ineptum & absurdum, quod possit facile & traducere, & refellere.
latin.669: Argumentor a verbis Apostoli. Quaeritur quod peccatum sit intelligendum, cum dicit Apostolus, Per unum hominem peccatum introivit in mundum, & per peccatum mors. Item, eo quod omnes peccaverunt. Aio, illud idem intelligendum esse, quod significatur verbis seqq. Nam usque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo. Negatne, an concedit Vir doctus? Concedere videtur. Subsumo igitur, Atqui verbis illis significatur peccatum habituale: id enim fuit in mundo, hoc est, in hominibus usque ad legem, nonne? Quid est in hoc meo argumento, quod reprehendi possit. Illud quaeso relege, ut est in manuscripto, & expende, lector aequissime, aut etiam ut recitatum est a Viro docto.
latin.670: GAR. 3. Sed objectio facile utrinque solvetur si distinctione utamur. Nam in obedientia quidem Christi distinguendus est actus a fructu, & existentia ab imputatione. Etsi enim obedientia illa actualis non est amplius ratione actus & existentiae, perdurat tamen, & perseverabit usque ad finem seculi ratione imputationis & fructus, quatenus eius obedientia iusti constituuntur multi. Rom. v. 19. Sic in Adami peccato illo primo distingui par est actum a reatu: ut dicamus, actum quidem non durasse usque ad legem, cum momento transierit, sed reatum perseveraturum usque ad mundi finem, quippe cum descendat in unumquemque naturalium Adae posterorum: Reatus enim ex uno venit in omnes in condemnationem, Rom. v. 16.

pass_a.665: Garissoles: we easily slip these snares. Point 1: that Rom. 5:13 confirms what the prior verse said—all sinned in Adam—is granted; and those words, he says, teach imputation of Adam’s actual disobedience. So the reason Paul confirms and clarifies in v. 13 cannot fail to favor imputation.
pass_a.666: Placeus: how empty those reasons are we take ourselves to have made plain by our replies and arguments, so that no room for doubt remains.
pass_a.667: Garissoles’ second thrust: the duration argument used against imputing Adam’s sin could as well be used against imputing Christ’s actual obedience—if Adam’s disobedience was not imputed until the law because it did not last until the law, why may one not also say Christ’s obedience unto death cannot be imputed to us because it did not last until our times?
pass_a.668: Placeus denies the rewrite: he did not conclude that Adam’s disobedience was unimputed until the law because it did not endure until the law. The learned man turns an invincible argument into a silly absurdity he can then brand and refute.
pass_a.669: Placeus argues from Paul’s words: what sin is meant when Paul says sin entered through one man, and death through sin, and that all sinned? The same sin named in the following words—until the law sin was in the world. The opponent seems to grant that. Subsumption: those words mean habitual sin, for that was in men until the law. What in this argument can be blamed? Reread it in the manuscript, fair reader.
pass_a.670: Garissoles’ third: solve both sides by distinction. In Christ’s obedience separate the act from the fruit, and existence from imputation—the actual obedience no longer exists as act, yet endures to the age’s end by imputation and fruit (Rom 5:19). Likewise in Adam’s first sin separate the act from the guilt: the act passed in a moment and did not last until the law, but the reatus perseveres to the world’s end as it descends on each natural descendant (Rom 5:16).

665: GAR. We will easily extricate ourselves from these snares.
For, first: that by these words the Apostle confirms what he had said in the preceding verse is confessed, as we have already heard.
But he had said that all sinned in Adam—by which words, by clear reasons, we have maintained that the imputation of Adam’s actual disobedience is taught.
Therefore the reason by which the Apostle confirms and clarifies that in this verse 13 cannot fail to be favorable to imputation.
666: PLAC. But as for how null those reasons are, we judge that we have made it so clear by our replies and our reasons that no place of doubting remains.
667: GAR. 2. The argument which is here used against the imputation of Adam’s sin, someone could use no less against the imputation of Christ’s actual obedience.

For if it is rightly gathered that Adam’s disobedience was not imputed until the law, because it did not endure until the law: why may it not also be legitimately gathered that Christ’s actual obedience, by which he showed himself obedient unto death, can in no way be imputed to us, because it did not last until our times?
668: PLAC. I did not gather that Adam’s disobedience was not imputed until the law because it did not endure until the law.
My argument, which is invincible, the learned man transforms into another, inept and absurd, which he can then easily both traduce and refute.
669: I argue from the Apostle’s words.
The question is what sin is to be understood when the Apostle says, Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death—and likewise, in that all sinned.
I say that the same is to be understood which is signified by the following words: For until the law sin was in the world.
Does the learned man deny, or concede? He seems to concede.
I therefore subsume: But by those words habitual sin is signified; for that was in the world, that is, in men, until the law—was it not?
What is there in this argument of mine that can be blamed? I ask you to reread it as it stands in the manuscript, and weigh it, most fair reader—or even as it was recited by the learned man.
670: GAR. 3. But the objection will easily be solved on both sides if we use a distinction.
For in Christ’s obedience the act is to be distinguished from the fruit, and existence from imputation.

For although that actual obedience no longer is, as to act and existence, yet it endures, and will persevere to the end of the age, as to imputation and fruit, insofar as by his obedience many are constituted righteous (Rom. 5:19).

So in that first sin of Adam it is fair to distinguish the act from the guilt: that we may say the act indeed did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment, but that the guilt will persevere to the end of the world, seeing that it descends upon each of Adam’s natural posterity.
For guilt came from one upon all unto condemnation (Rom. 5:16).
